# Errors and I/O

**Audience:** Edva users<br>
**Status:** current guide<br>
**Audited:** `8b8cb19`<br>
**Evidence:** `std/io.dva`, `prelude.dva`, `process/spec/ramifications.md`,
`tests/pass/220_stdio.dva`

Edva represents recoverable failure with ramifications rather than a hidden
exception mechanism. A fallible operation returns a ram whose slots describe
success and failure. For example, container lookup returns `< Value | Error >`
and the buffered input operations in `io` return `< String | >` at end of
input.

## Handle an expected absence

Use a positional choice when both outcomes are meaningful. The first bare
branch receives the first slot; the second receives the second slot.

```dva
#type Lookup < Int | >

report: Lookup => ()
report = result =>
   result
      | value => print_int(value)
      | _ => print("missing")
```

`Error` is special: it can be constructed directly only as an error payload.
Unwrapping an error aborts after printing its diagnostic information, so an
`Error` payload is not recoverable application data. For a success value that
must exist, use postfix `!!`; it extracts the first payload or aborts on the
other slot.

```dva
value = table ^ "answer"
print_int(value!!)
```

Do not use a fake `| 0` fallback merely to make a statement choice exhaustive.
An assignment and a statement choice produce Unit, so they already fit a
side-effect-only function with a `=> ()` signature.

## Write to standard streams

The prelude loads `io` automatically and exposes `print` and typed helpers.
Import `io` directly when choosing an output descriptor or formatting values.

```dva
#use io

io::out("ready")
io::err("unable to continue")
io::outf(("items", 3), "{}: {}")
```

`io::out` and `io::err` write a formatted value followed by a newline.
`io::outf` and `io::errf` replace `{}` placeholders from one value or the
fields of a record, in order. `io::STDIN`, `io::STDOUT`, and `io::STDERR` are
the standard file descriptors.

## Read until EOF

Create an `io::Reader` for a descriptor. Each read operation returns a
positive payload when data is available and a unit second slot at EOF, so EOF
is normal control flow rather than an `Error` payload.

```dva
#use io

reader = io::reader(io::STDIN)
chunk = io::read(reader, 4096)
chunk | text => print(text) | _ => print("end of input")
```

`io::read_all`, `io::read_byte`, `io::read_until`, and `io::read_line` follow
the same ram-based EOF convention. See the [`io` reference](../reference/stdlib/io.qmd)
for their result types and buffer-capacity options.
